The first morning without the bus, Arthur walked the route.

He left his house at six twelve, carrying a thermos and wearing the blue jacket with the transit company’s name removed. The stitching remained, a pale rectangle above his heart.

At the corner of Bell and Mercer, he stopped beside the empty shelter.

“Morning,” said Mrs. Alvarez.

“Morning.”

“They’ve discontinued it.”

“I know.”

She looked down the road anyway. She had a shopping trolley with one wheel that pointed permanently toward the church.

Arthur checked his watch.

After a moment, he said, “I’m walking.”

“To the hospital?”

“As far as the depot.”

She considered this, then pulled her trolley into line beside him.

They passed the bakery before its lights came on. They passed the insurance office with the dead fern. At the second stop, a boy in kitchen whites was sitting on the curb, looking at his phone.

“No bus,” he said without looking up.

“No,” Arthur agreed.

The boy stood and came with them.

By the time they reached the bridge, there were six.

Arthur knew how long the route took in rain, in snow, with school traffic, with the market spilling illegally across the turning lane. He knew where passengers began reaching for the bell. He knew which pothole could make a sleeping person bite their tongue.

Walking, he discovered that the bridge smelled of wet iron.

He had crossed it eleven times a day for twenty-three years.

He had never known its smell.

***

On Tuesday, Mrs. Alvarez brought a bag of peppermints.

On Wednesday, the boy in kitchen whites introduced himself as Dev and explained that he was not a chef, despite what everyone assumed. He washed dishes at the hotel.

“Temporarily,” he added.

Nobody asked what came afterward.

On Thursday, it rained.

Arthur expected to walk alone, but Mrs. Alvarez was waiting in a yellow cape. Dev had an umbrella advertising an expensive champagne he had never tasted.

At the third stop, they found a woman holding two coffees.

“I didn’t know if you’d come,” she told Arthur.

“Neither did I.”

She gave him one.

***

By the second week, people had begun calling it the walking bus.

Arthur disliked the name. A bus was a machine designed to prevent precisely this amount of walking.

Still, he found himself keeping time.

They left Bell and Mercer at six twenty. They waited no more than two minutes at the pharmacy. At the bridge, they slowed for Mr. Okafor, whose left knee had developed an opinion about slopes.

People joined and departed. They carried lunch bags, flowers, legal papers, shoes for work. One morning, a man carried a small aquarium with no fish in it.

“Moving?” Dev asked.

“Divorce.”

They walked quietly with him for three blocks.

***

The letter from the council arrived in October.

Arthur read it twice at his kitchen table.

It thanked him for his community spirit. It described the walking bus as an inspiring example of resilience. It asked whether he would agree to a photograph for the borough newsletter.

He put the letter beneath the short leg of the table.

The table still rocked.

He folded it once more.

***

His daughter called on Sunday.

“You’re doing their job for them,” she said.

“I’m walking.”

“You know what I mean.”

He did.

She lived three hundred miles away in a city where buses arrived so frequently that people complained when two came together.

“Dad, you’re allowed to be angry.”

“I am angry.”

“You don’t sound angry.”

He looked at his jacket hanging on the chair. The pale rectangle had begun collecting dust along its upper seam.

“I can be angry at four miles an hour.”

After she laughed, he realized he had been waiting all week to make someone laugh.

***

In November, Mrs. Alvarez stopped coming.

For three mornings, Arthur waited the full two minutes at Bell and Mercer.

On the fourth, he went to her building.

She opened the door in slippers.

“Nothing dramatic,” she said immediately. “My hip.”

Behind her, the television showed a bright beach without sound.

“You should have told us.”

“And then what?”

He had no answer ready. It bothered him how often this happened now that he was no longer separated from people by a steering wheel.

She let him in.

Her shopping list lay on the table, written on the back of a birthday card.

He took it.

***

That winter, the route changed.

It bent toward Mrs. Alvarez’s building on Tuesdays and Fridays. It detoured past the cheaper grocer. When Dev found work at a different hotel, they moved the departure time forward ten minutes.

Arthur bought a notebook.

On its first page he wrote names and telephone numbers. On the second, he wrote who had a car, who could drive at night, who needed help on stairs.

He drew no map.

***

In March, a reporter came.

She asked Arthur to stand beside the abandoned bus shelter.

“Could you look hopeful?” she said.

He tried.

She lowered her camera.

“Maybe just natural.”

That was harder.

The article appeared beneath the headline THE TOWN THAT KEPT MOVING.

Arthur bought a copy, read it, and telephoned the reporter.

“You left out the part about restoring the service.”

“We had limited space.”

“That was the part I wanted in.”

***

The bus returned in June, smaller and less frequent.

On its first morning, Arthur boarded behind Mrs. Alvarez. She paid her fare, then turned to watch him take out his wallet.

“Strange?” she asked.

“A bit.”

They sat together near the back. At the bridge, Dev waved from the pavement, already halfway to work.

Arthur lifted his hand.

He had brought the notebook. Before his stop, he checked Friday’s shopping list with Mrs. Alvarez.

Then he reached for the bell.
